# The provenance file on Ꜣḫ

*Provenance record 016 · Ꜣḫ · one temple, fully accounted for.*

## Provenance

**1. The attestation.** **𓅜𓏤**, from the tradition's own record. On record: Pyramid Texts, Utterance 263 (Faulkner, The Ancient Egyptian Pyramid Texts, 1969)., Book of the Dead, Spells 89, 97, and 130 (Faulkner, The Ancient Egyptian Book of the Dead, 1972; Allen, The Egyptian Book of the Dead, 2015)., Gardiner, A. H., and K. Sethe, Letters to the Dead (Egyptian Exploration Society, 1928); Wente, Letters from Ancient Egypt (1990)., Plutarch, On Isis and Osiris (the Greco-Roman outsider's account of Egyptian soul-doctrine)..

**2. The narrative record.** **The King Ascends as an Akh** — In the Pyramid Texts, the oldest corpus of Egyptian religious literature, the king is repeatedly assured that he will ascend to the sky as an akh.  Utterance 263 declares that he goes “as an akh, as lord of the horizon,” joining Re in his solar barque and taking his place among the circumpolar stars — the imperishable ones, who never set into the underworld. **The Transfiguration Spells** — The Book of the Dead treats akh-hood as its goal-state.  Spell 97 exists “for causing a man to be an akh in the realm of the dead”; Spell 130 gathers the disparate parts of the deceased's being into an effective akh with an eternal ba; and the rubrics of other spells are “for making a spirit excellent” — in Egyptian, sꜣḫ, the causative of the very word ꜣḫ.

**3. The physical record.** The akh is attested in tomb inscriptions, coffin panels, and papyri from the Old Kingdom through the Ptolemaic period. Pyramid Texts utterances on Fifth- and Sixth-Dynasty royal pyramids at Saqqara describe the king ascending as an akh to join the circumpolar stars; New Kingdom Book of the Dead vignettes — above all Spell 89's human-headed bird hovering over the mummy in papyri such as the Papyrus of Ani (British Museum EA10470) — show the reunion of ba and body. Heart scarabs of green stone, set over the chest with Spell 30B, protected the transformed spirit at the weighing of the heart, and letters to the dead on bowls and stelae (Cairo, Naga ed-Deir, Coptos) preserve the ancestors' correspondence. The material record is the doctrine made portable: amulets a hand could hold, spells a wall could carry.

**4. The current holding.** The temple at [/akh/](/akh/), classified Tier 1. The restoration preserves more than the ASCII form can express — stress, length, or a letter the Latin keyboard lost — which places it, mechanically, in Tier-1.

**5. The documented resonances.** **Funerary & Memorial Services**, **Biotech, Longevity & Life Sciences**, **Mental Health & Emotional Wellness** — seats argued and weighted in the [pattern atlas](/patterns/), read through the myths in this temple's [Resonance File](/akh/blog/resonance/).

**6. The primary sources.** [The Book of the Dead](/texts/book-of-the-dead/) — the library this file answers to, open at the [Sacred Texts collection](/texts/).

**7. The continuing record.** The akh is one of Egypt's most durable exports.  Every museum with an Egyptian collection displays its technology — heart scarabs, Book of the Dead papyri such as the Papyrus of Ani (British Museum EA10470), offering stelae — and every visitor who reads a curse against the tomb-robber meets the doctrine: the name and the provisions are the dead person's continued agency.
